Some, however, from the Pharisees’ sect who had come to believe stood up and declared, “They must be circumcised, and charged to observe Moses’ Law.”
So the apostles and elders met together to consider this question.

After there had been much debate, Peter rose and said to them, “Brothers, you are aware that in early days God made his choice among you, that by my mouth the Gentiles should hear the word of the gospel and believe.
And God, the knower of hearts, testified for them, granting them the Holy Spirit even as he granted him to us;
and he set no difference at all between them and us, when by faith he purified their hearts.
Now, then, why are you putting God to the test by laying on the neck of the disciples a yoke that neither our fathers nor we have had strength to bear?
No — it is through the grace of the Lord Jesus that we believe we are saved, in the same way as they.”
The whole assembly fell silent, and they listened while Barnabas and Paul related what signs and wonders God had done among the Gentiles through them.
After they finished speaking, James answered, “Brothers, hear me.
Simeon{b} has related how God first took thought to take from among the Gentiles a people for his name.
With this the words of the prophets agree, as it stands written,

‘After this I will return,
and I will rebuild the fallen tent of David;
its ruins I will rebuild,
and I will set it upright again,

that those remaining of mankind may search out the Lord,
and every nation upon whom my name is called,
says the Lord, who does these things,
known from of old.’{c}
My judgment, therefore, is that we should not make trouble for those among the Gentiles who are turning to God,
but should write to them to keep away from the pollutions of idols and from sexual immorality and from what is strangled and from blood.{d}
For Moses, from ancient generations, has had in every city those who proclaim him, being read in the synagogues every sabbath.”

Then it seemed good to the apostles and the elders, with the whole church, to choose men from among them and send them to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas — Judas called Barsabbas,{e} and Silas,{f} leading men among the brothers —

with this letter in their hand:{g}
“The apostles and the elders, your brothers, to the brothers of Gentile origin in Antioch and Syria and Cilicia: greetings.
Since we have heard that certain persons from among us, to whom we gave no instructions, have unsettled you with words, upsetting your minds,{h}
we have resolved, having come to one mind, to choose men and send them to you along with our beloved Barnabas and Paul,
men who have handed over their lives for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.
We have therefore sent Judas and Silas, who will tell you the same things by word of mouth.
For it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to lay upon you no further burden than these necessary things:
keep away from food offered to idols, from blood, from things strangled, and from fornication. Guard yourselves against these and it will be well with you.{i} Be strong in health.”
So when they had been sent off, they went down to Antioch, and having gathered the assembly together, they delivered the letter.
And when they had read it, they rejoiced at the encouragement.
And Judas and Silas, who were themselves also prophets, encouraged the brothers with many words and strengthened them.
And when they had passed some time there, the brothers released them with a blessing of peace to return to the ones who sent them.
But Paul and Barnabas stayed on in Antioch, teaching and proclaiming, with many others also, the word of the Lord.
After some days Paul said to Barnabas, “Come, let us go back and visit the brothers in every city where we proclaimed the word of the Lord, and see how they are.”
Barnabas wanted to take along with them John also, who was called Mark.
Paul, however, did not consider it fitting to bring along the man who had deserted them back in Pamphylia and had not stayed with them for the work.
And there arose a sharp disagreement, so that they parted company; Barnabas took Mark and sailed off to Cyprus,
but Paul chose Silas and departed, commended by the brothers to the grace of the Lord.{k}
And he went through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the churches.

notes.text: Codex Bezae adds “and walk according to the custom of Moses,” and in 15:2 says that Paul had told them to remain as they were when they believed.
Simeon: Peter’s Hebrew name, Shimon, “he has heard.”

Amos 9:11–12 (Greek), with Isa 45:21. The Hebrew of Amos 9:12 reads “that they may possess the remnant of Edom.” For “known from of old,” many later manuscripts read “Known to God from of old are all his works.”

The Western text (Codex Bezae and others) omits “what is strangled” here and in 15:29, and adds the negative Golden Rule: “and not to do to others what they would not want done to themselves.” This turns the decree from food laws into moral precepts (idolatry, immorality, bloodshed).
Barsabbas: probably “son of the sabbath”; the meaning is uncertain.
Silas: a Semitic name, perhaps from Aramaic *sheila*, “asked”; Paul calls him Silvanus (1 Thess 1:1). The meaning is uncertain.
With this letter in their hand: literally “having written by their hand.”
Many later manuscripts add “saying, ‘You must be circumcised and keep the Law.’”
You will do well: Codex Bezae adds “being borne along by the Holy Spirit.”

Verse 34: the Westcott–Hort text and the earliest manuscripts do not include verse 34; the number is kept here only to preserve the traditional verse numbering. Some manuscripts, including Codex Bezae and Ephraemi, add “But it seemed good to Silas to remain there,” and Bezae continues, “and Judas journeyed alone.” The addition explains why Silas is in Antioch in 15:40.
Of the Lord: many manuscripts read “of God.”

verses.text: He arrived too at Derbe, and at Lystra. A certain disciple was there by the name of Timothy,{a} whose mother was a believing Jewess, while his father was Greek.
The brothers in Lystra and Iconium gave a good report of him.
Paul wanted him to go with him; and he took him and circumcised him on account of the Jews who were in those places, for they all knew that his father was a Greek.
As they went on their way through the cities, they delivered to them for observance the decisions reached by the apostles and elders who were in Jerusalem.
So the churches were strengthened in the faith and grew in numbers daily.
They went through the region of Phrygia and Galatia,{b} having been forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia.{c}
When they had come opposite Mysia, they tried to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus{d} did not allow them.
So, passing by Mysia, they went down to Troas.
And a vision appeared to Paul in the night: a man of Macedonia was standing there, pleading with him and saying, “Cross over into Macedonia and help us.”
When he had seen the vision, immediately we{e} sought to go on into Macedonia, concluding that God had called us to proclaim the good news to them.
Setting sail, then, from Troas, we ran a straight course to Samothrace, and the following day to Neapolis,
and thence to Philippi, foremost city of that part of Macedonia,{f} a Roman colony. Some days we spent in this city.
And on the sabbath day we went outside the gate beside a river, where we supposed there was a place of prayer;{g} and sitting down, we spoke to the women who had come together.
Among our hearers was a God-fearing woman by the name of Lydia,{h} a seller of purple goods, from the city of Thyatira, whose heart the Lord opened to give heed to Paul’s words.
And when she had been baptized, and her household, she urged us, saying, “If you have judged me to be faithful to the Lord, come into my house and stay.” And she prevailed on us.
Once, on our way to the place of prayer, we encountered a slave girl possessed by a spirit of divination,{i} who by her soothsaying brought her masters large profits.
She kept following Paul and us, crying out, “These men are servants of the Most High God, who proclaim to you a way of salvation.”
This she kept doing for many days. Paul, greatly annoyed, turned and said to the spirit, “I command you in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her.” And it came out that very hour.
Her masters, seeing that the hope of their profits had departed, laid hold of Paul and Silas and hauled them to the marketplace in front of the authorities.
And having brought them to the magistrates,{j} they said, “These men are throwing our city into an uproar. They are Jews,
and they teach practices that we, being Romans, are not permitted to adopt or to observe.”
The mob also rose up together against them, and the magistrates ripped their clothes from them and ordered them flogged with rods.
And when they had inflicted many blows on them, they threw them into prison, ordering the jailer to keep them securely.
He, on receiving an order like this, cast them into the innermost cell and made their feet fast in the wooden stocks.
About midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the prisoners were listening to them,
and suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken; and [immediately] all the doors were opened, and everyone’s bonds were unfastened.
When the jailer woke and saw the prison doors open, he drew his sword and was about to kill himself, supposing that the prisoners had escaped.
But Paul called out with a loud voice, “Do yourself no harm, for we are all here.”
Calling for lights, the jailer sprang inside and, quaking, threw himself down before Paul and Silas.
Then he brought them out and said, “Sirs, what must I do to be saved?”
And they said, “Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household.”
And they spoke the word of the Lord{k} to him and to all who were in his house.
And taking them at that hour of the night, he bathed the stripes from their backs; and immediately he was baptized, he and all who were his.
Then, leading them up into his home, he spread a table before them, and with all his house he was full of joy at having come to believe in God.
But when it was day, the magistrates sent the police{l} with the message, “Let those men go.”
And the jailer reported these words to Paul: “The magistrates have sent word to let you go. So come out now and go in peace.”

But Paul answered them, “Without a trial they flogged us in public, Roman citizens though we are, and cast us into prison — and are they now to put us out quietly? Not at all! Let them come in person and escort us out.”
The police reported these words to the magistrates, and they were afraid when they heard that they were Roman citizens.
So they came and pleaded with them, and bringing them out, they begged them to depart from the city.{m}
So they went out of the prison and visited Lydia. And when they had seen the brothers, they encouraged them and departed.

notes.text: Timothy: Greek, “honoring God.”
The region of Phrygia and Galatia: or “Phrygia and the Galatian region.”
Asia: the Roman province in western Asia Minor.
The Spirit of Jesus: this unusual expression is in the earliest manuscripts; later manuscripts read simply “the Spirit.”
We: here the first of the “we” passages in Acts begins (16:10–17; 20:5–21:18; 27:1–28:16), traditionally taken to mean the author joined Paul.

A leading city of the district of Macedonia: so the Westcott–Hort text (literally “first city of the part of Macedonia”); the Greek is difficult, and some editors adopt a conjectural reading, “a city of the first district of Macedonia.” Macedonia was divided into four districts.
Place of prayer: Greek *proseuchē*, often used of a synagogue.
Lydia: a name meaning “the Lydian woman”; Thyatira was in the region of Lydia.
A spirit of divination: literally “a spirit, a python,” after the serpent Python of the oracle at Delphi.
Magistrates: Greek *stratēgoi*, the chief officials of the colony.
Police: Greek *rhabdouchoi*, “rod-bearers,” the attendants of the magistrates (Latin *lictores*).
Of the Lord: some early manuscripts read “of God.”

Codex Bezae greatly expands 16:35–40: the magistrates come “to the market place” and, “remembering the earthquake,” are afraid; they beg Paul and Silas, “We did not know the truth about you, that you are righteous men,” and ask them to leave lest the crowd turn on them again.

verses.text: Taking the road through Amphipolis and Apollonia, they arrived at Thessalonica, where the Jews had a synagogue.
Paul, as his habit was, went in among them, and over three sabbaths he reasoned with them out of the Scriptures,
opening them up and setting forth that it was necessary for the Messiah to suffer and to rise from the dead, and that “this Jesus, whom I announce to you, is the Messiah.”
Some of them were convinced and threw in their lot with Paul and Silas, as did a great crowd of God-fearing Greeks and not a few of the foremost women.

But the Jews grew jealous, and taking along some wicked fellows from the marketplace rabble, they gathered a mob and set the city in an uproar. They descended on Jason’s{a} house, seeking to bring Paul and Silas out to the people’s assembly.{b}
Not finding them there, they dragged Jason and certain brothers before the city officials,{c} bawling out, “These men who have turned the world upside down have come here too,
and Jason has taken them in! They all act against the decrees of Caesar, saying there is another king, Jesus.”
At these words both the crowd and the politarchs became agitated;
and only after taking security from Jason and the others did they let them go.
Immediately, under cover of night, the brothers sent Paul and Silas away to Beroea, and on their arrival there they went off to the synagogue of the Jews.
These Jews were of nobler mind than those in Thessalonica: they took in the word with all eagerness, sifting the Scriptures day after day to see whether these things held true.
Many of them, therefore, became believers, along with no small number of Greek women of standing and of men.
But once the Jews of Thessalonica learned that the word of God had been proclaimed by Paul in Beroea too, there also they came, agitating and stirring up the crowds.
Then the brothers at once sent Paul off to make his way to the sea, while Silas and Timothy stayed behind there.
Those who escorted Paul brought him as far as Athens; and with instructions for Silas and Timothy to join him with all possible speed, they departed.
Now while Paul waited for them in Athens, his spirit was roused within him as he saw that the city was full of idols.
So he held discussions in the synagogue with the Jews and the God-fearers, and in the marketplace every day with whoever chanced to be there.

Some of the Epicurean and Stoic philosophers also engaged him in debate. And some were saying, “What would this seed-picker{d} wish to say?” Others, “He seems to be a herald of foreign divinities” — because he was preaching Jesus and the resurrection.{e}
So they took hold of him and brought him to the Areopagus,{f} saying, “May we learn what this new teaching is that you are presenting?
For you are bringing some strange notions to our ears; we want, then, to know what these things mean.”
(Now all the Athenians and the foreigners residing there had leisure for nothing else than telling or hearing something newer.)

So Paul, standing in the midst of the Areopagus, said:
“Men of Athens, I observe that in every way you are exceedingly religious.{g}

For as I was passing through and looking over the objects of your worship, I found also an altar on which had been inscribed, ‘To an unknown god.’ What therefore you worship without knowing, this I announce to you.
The God who made the world and all that is in it — he, being Lord of heaven and earth, does not dwell in shrines made by hands,
nor is he waited on by human hands as if he lacked anything, since he himself gives to all life and breath and all things.
And from one{h} he made every nation of humankind to dwell on all the face of the earth, having fixed appointed seasons and the boundaries of their habitation,
that they should seek God, if perhaps they might grope for him and find him — though indeed he is not far from each one of us.

For in him we live and move and have our being; as also some of your own poets have said,
‘For we too are his offspring.’{i}
Being, then, God’s offspring, we ought not to think the divine nature is like gold or silver or stone, a thing engraved by human art and imagination.
God, then, has looked past the times of not knowing; but at present he is announcing to humanity that everyone in every place must repent,
because he has set a day on which he is about to judge the inhabited world in righteousness by a man whom he has designated, having furnished proof to all by raising him from the dead.”
When they heard of a resurrection of the dead, some began to scoff; but others said, “We will hear you on this subject another time.”
So Paul went out from among them.
But certain men joined him and believed, among them Dionysius the Areopagite{j} and a woman named Damaris,{k} and others with them.

notes.text: Jason: a Greek name, “healer,” often used by Jews named Joshua (Jesus).
People’s assembly: Greek *dēmos*, the citizen body of a free city; or simply “the crowd.”
City officials: Greek *politarchas*, “politarchs,” the title of the magistrates of Thessalonica, attested in inscriptions.
Seed-picker: Greek *spermologos*, a bird that picks up seeds; used of an idle babbler who picks up scraps of learning.
Jesus and the resurrection: some hearers may have taken “Resurrection” (*Anastasis*) as the name of a goddess paired with Jesus.
Areopagus: “hill of Ares,” the Greek god of war; also the name of the council that met there.
Exceedingly religious: or “very superstitious”; Greek *deisidaimonesterous*.
From one: many later manuscripts read “from one blood.”
The words “in him we live and move and have our being” are thought to echo the Cretan poet Epimenides; the quoted line is from Aratus, *Phaenomena* 5.
Areopagite: a member of the council of the Areopagus.
Damaris: the meaning is uncertain; perhaps a form of *damalis*, “heifer.” Codex Bezae omits her name.

verses.text: After this Paul left Athens and came to Corinth.
There he came upon a Jew named Aquila,{a} a native of Pontus, lately arrived from Italy with Priscilla{b} his wife because Claudius had ordered all the Jews to leave Rome.{c} He went to see them,
and since their craft was his own he lodged with them and they plied it together; tentmaking{d} was their trade.
And every sabbath he would argue in the synagogue, trying to persuade Jews and Greeks.
When Silas and Timothy came down from Macedonia, Paul was wholly absorbed with the word, testifying to the Jews that the Messiah was Jesus.
And when they set themselves against him and spoke abusively, he shook out his garments and said to them, “Your blood be on your own heads! I am clean. From now on I will go to the Gentiles.”
Moving on from there, he entered the home of one Titius Justus,{e} a God-fearer, whose house stood next door to the synagogue.
Crispus,{f} the synagogue ruler, came to believe in the Lord, along with all his household; and many of the Corinthians who heard believed and were baptized.
Then the Lord said to Paul one night in a vision, “Have no fear; keep on speaking, and do not be silent,
for I am with you, and no one shall lay a hand on you to harm you, because I have many people in this city.”
So he settled there a year and six months, teaching the word of God among them.
But when Gallio was proconsul of Achaia,{g} the Jews rose up in concert against Paul and brought him before the judgment seat,
and charging, “This man is inducing people to revere God against the law.”
Paul was about to open his mouth when Gallio said to the Jews, “If it were some misdeed or vicious crime, O Jews, I would have reason to bear with you;
but if these are questions about words and names and your own law, see to it yourselves. A judge of such matters I refuse to be.”
So he had them driven from the tribunal.
Then they all{h} seized Sosthenes, the synagogue ruler, and beat him in front of the judgment seat. But Gallio paid no attention to any of this.
Paul remained many days more, then bade the brothers farewell and set sail for Syria, Priscilla and Aquila with him, having shorn his head at Cenchreae, since he had taken a vow.{i}
They came to Ephesus, and he left them there; but he himself went into the synagogue and reasoned with the Jews.
They pressed him to remain longer, but he would not consent;
but on taking leave of them he said, “I will come back to you again, if God wills,”{j} and he set sail from Ephesus.
When he had landed at Caesarea, he went up{k} and greeted the church, and then went down to Antioch.
Having spent a while there, he set out and passed in turn through the Galatian country and Phrygia, giving strength to all the disciples.
Meanwhile there arrived at Ephesus a certain Jew, Apollos{l} by name, Alexandrian by birth, a learned man and mighty in the Scriptures.
He had been instructed in the Way of the Lord; and being fervent in spirit, he spoke and taught accurately the things concerning Jesus, though he knew only the baptism of John.
He began to speak out boldly in the synagogue; but when Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside and explained to him the Way of God{m} more accurately.
He wanted to go across into Achaia, so the brothers urged him on and wrote asking the disciples to receive him. After he came, he was of great service to the ones who by grace had come to believe;{n}
for with force he confuted the Jews openly, demonstrating from the Scriptures that the Messiah was Jesus.

notes.text: Aquila: Latin, “eagle.”
Priscilla: a diminutive of the Latin Prisca, “ancient, venerable.”
The emperor Claudius expelled Jews from Rome about AD 49 (Suetonius, *Claudius* 25.4).
Tentmakers: Greek *skēnopoioi*; possibly “leatherworkers.”
Titius Justus: so the Westcott–Hort text, with Vaticanus; Sinaiticus reads “Titus Justus,” and many manuscripts simply “Justus.”
Crispus: Latin, “curly.”
Gallio … proconsul of Achaia: Lucius Junius Gallio, brother of the philosopher Seneca; an inscription at Delphi places his proconsulship in AD 51–52.
They all: many later manuscripts read “all the Greeks.”
He was under a vow: probably a Nazirite vow or one like it (Num 6:1–21); grammatically, the one who cut his hair might be Aquila.
If God wills: many later manuscripts, following Codex Bezae, add before this, “I must by all means keep the coming feast in Jerusalem.”
He went up: that is, to Jerusalem.
Apollos: short for Apollonius, from the god Apollo.
The Way of God: some manuscripts read “the Way of the Lord,” and others “the Way.”
Codex Bezae rewrites 18:27, saying that some Corinthians staying in Ephesus urged Apollos to come to their country.

verses.text: It came about, while Apollos was at Corinth, that Paul, having passed through the inland regions,{a} came down to Ephesus, where he found certain disciples.
“Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you came to believe?” he asked them. They replied, “No — we have not so much as heard whether there is a Holy Spirit.”
“Into what, then, were you baptized?” he said. “Into John’s baptism,” said they.
Paul answered, “John’s was a baptism of repentance; he told the people that their faith must rest on him who was to come after — on Jesus, that is.”
On hearing this, they were baptized into the name of the Lord Jesus.
And when Paul had laid his hands upon them, the Holy Spirit came on them, and they began speaking in tongues and prophesying.
There were about twelve men in all.
He went into the synagogue and for three months spoke out boldly, debating and persuading about the kingdom of God.

But when some grew hardened and would not believe, maligning the Way before the gathering, he withdrew from them, took the disciples apart with him, and day by day held discussions in the lecture hall of Tyrannus.{b}
This went on for two years, so that every inhabitant of Asia, Jew and Greek, heard the word of the Lord.
And God was working miracles of no ordinary kind by Paul’s hands,
so much so that cloths and aprons{c} were taken from his body to those who were ill, and they were rid of their sicknesses and the wicked spirits departed.
Then some of the itinerant Jewish exorcists also undertook to pronounce the name of the Lord Jesus over those who had the evil spirits, saying, “I adjure you by the Jesus whom Paul preaches.”
Seven sons of a certain Sceva, a Jewish high priest,{d} were doing this.
But the evil spirit retorted to them, “Jesus I know, and Paul I am acquainted with; but you — who are you?”
Then the man in whom the evil spirit was leaped on them, overpowered them both,{e} and so prevailed against them that they fled out of that house naked and wounded.
This became known to all the residents of Ephesus, Jews and Greeks alike; fear fell upon them all, and the name of the Lord Jesus was held in high honor.
Many of those who had believed now came forward, confessing and disclosing their practices.{f}

And a good number of those who had practiced magic arts brought their books together and burned them in the sight of all. When they reckoned up the value of them, it came to fifty thousand days’ wages.{g}
So mightily did the word of the Lord grow and prevail.
When all this was accomplished, Paul purposed in the Spirit{h} to travel by way of Macedonia and Achaia to Jerusalem, saying, “After I have been there, I must see Rome as well.”
And having sent into Macedonia two of his helpers, Timothy and Erastus,{i} he himself stayed on in Asia for a time.
About that time there arose no small disturbance concerning the Way.
For a silversmith named Demetrius, who made [silver] shrines of Artemis,{j} was bringing the craftsmen no small business.
Calling them together with the workmen in related trades, he said, “Men, you know that our prosperity comes from this business.

You are looking on and hearing how, not at Ephesus only but over nearly the whole of Asia, this Paul has won over a sizable crowd and led them astray, by telling them that handmade gods are no gods at all.

It is not merely this line of ours that risks falling into contempt; the sanctuary of the mighty goddess Artemis also stands to be reckoned as nothing, and she is about to be stripped of her majesty, she whom the whole of Asia and the world revere.”
When they heard this, they were filled with rage and kept shouting, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!”
So the whole city was filled with turmoil, and with one impulse they surged into the theater, seizing as they went Gaius and Aristarchus,{k} Macedonians traveling with Paul.
Paul wanted to go in among the people, but the disciples would not let him;
and even some of the officials of the province,{l} who were friends of his, sent to him and urged him not to venture into the theater.
Now some were crying one thing, some another; the assembly was a confused mass, and the greater part had no idea for what purpose they had assembled.
Some in the crowd instructed Alexander, since the Jews had thrust him to the front; and Alexander, waving his hand for silence, was ready to offer a defense before the populace.
But when they recognized that he was a Jew, a single cry went up from them all, and for about two hours they kept shouting, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!”
The town clerk{m} finally calmed the mob and said, “Ephesians, what man alive is unaware that Ephesus is guardian of the temple{n} of great Artemis and of the image fallen from heaven?{o}
Since, then, these things cannot be contradicted, you ought to be quiet and do nothing rash.
For you have brought these men here who are neither temple robbers nor blasphemers of our goddess.
So if Demetrius and his fellow craftsmen have a case against somebody, court days are held and proconsuls sit; let the parties bring their accusations there.
And should you want anything beyond that, the matter will be resolved in the regular assembly.
For we are in danger of being charged with rioting over today’s events, there being no cause that we can give to account for this commotion.”
And when he had said these things, he dismissed the assembly.

notes.text: The inland regions: literally “the upper parts,” the highlands of Asia Minor. Codex Bezae begins the verse: “But when Paul wished, according to his own plan, to go to Jerusalem, the Spirit told him to return to Asia.”

Tyrannus: Greek, “tyrant, ruler,” probably the owner of the hall or a teacher who lectured there. Codex Bezae adds “from eleven in the morning until four in the afternoon” (literally “from the fifth hour to the tenth”), the hours of the midday rest.
Handkerchiefs or aprons: Latin loanwords in Greek, *soudaria* and *simikinthia*; probably sweat cloths and work aprons.
A Jewish high priest: no Sceva is known among the high priests; he may have been of a high-priestly family or claimed the title.
Both: or “all of them”; the Greek *amphoterōn* sometimes means “all” in later Greek.
Practices: Greek *praxeis*, perhaps in the technical sense of magic spells.
Fifty thousand days’ wages: literally “fifty thousand of silver,” that is, silver coins, probably drachmas, each roughly a day’s wage for a laborer.
In the Spirit: or “in his spirit.”
Erastus: Greek, “beloved.”

Artemis: the Greek goddess identified with the Roman Diana; the Artemis of Ephesus was a mother goddess whose temple was one of the seven wonders of the world. The shrines were probably small models of the temple.
Gaius and Aristarchus: Gaius is a common Latin name; Aristarchus, Greek, “best ruler.”
Officials of the province: Greek *Asiarchōn*, “Asiarchs,” leading men of the province of Asia.
Town clerk: Greek *grammateus*, the chief civic official of Ephesus.
Temple keeper: Greek *neōkoros*, an honorary title of cities that maintained the temple of a deity or of the emperor.
The sacred stone that fell from the sky: literally “the fallen-from-Zeus [thing],” probably a meteorite venerated as an image of the goddess.

verses.text: When the uproar had ceased, Paul sent for the disciples and, after encouraging them, said farewell and set out for Macedonia.
When he had gone through those parts and had given them much encouragement, he came to Greece.
There he spent three months. And when a plot was made against him by the Jews as he was about to set sail for Syria, he decided to return through Macedonia.{a}
He was accompanied by Sopater the son of Pyrrhus, of Beroea; of the Thessalonians, Aristarchus and Secundus; Gaius of Derbe,{b} and Timothy; and from Asia, Tychicus and Trophimus.{c}
These went on ahead and were waiting for us at Troas;
As for us, we set sail out of Philippi once the days of Unleavened Bread were over, and five days later joined them in Troas, where we remained a week.
On the first day of the week, when we were gathered together to break bread, Paul talked with them, intending to depart on the next day, and he prolonged his speech until midnight.
There were many lamps in the upper room where we were gathered.
And a young man named Eutychus,{d} sitting at the window, was sinking into a deep sleep as Paul talked still longer. Overcome by sleep, he fell down from the third story{e} and was picked up dead.
Paul, however, went down, flung himself upon him, and clasping him said, “Stop your lamenting; his life is still in him.”
Then he climbed back up, broke the bread, and ate; and after speaking with them at length, till dawn, he left.
And they brought the lad home living, and were greatly comforted.
We, meanwhile, went before him to the ship and put out for Assos, where we were to pick Paul up; this was his arrangement, as he meant to make the journey on foot.
When he joined us at Assos, we took him aboard and came to Mitylene.
And sailing from there we came the following day opposite Chios; the next day we touched at Samos;{f} and the day after that we came to Miletus.
For Paul had determined to sail on past Ephesus and not lose time in Asia; he was pressing on, if at all possible, to be in Jerusalem for Pentecost day.
Now from Miletus he sent to Ephesus and called the elders of the church to come to him.

On their arrival he addressed them:
“You know well what my conduct was with you all along, from the day I first stepped into Asia:
slaving for the Lord in all lowliness of mind, in tears, and in the testings that came upon me from the Jews’ plotting;
how I held back nothing that would benefit you, but declared it to you and taught you openly and in your homes,
bearing solemn witness to Jews and Greeks alike of repentance toward God and faith in our Lord Jesus.{g}
And now, see, bound by the Spirit{h} I am on my way to Jerusalem, unaware of what I shall meet with there,
save that city after city the Holy Spirit warns me solemnly that chains and hardships lie in wait for me.
Yet I hold my life worth nothing, not precious to me at all, so long as I complete my race and the service the Lord Jesus entrusted to me, of bearing witness to the good news of God’s grace.{i}
And now, see, this I know: you will none of you look upon my face again — you all, among whom I went about heralding the kingdom.
For that reason I solemnly declare to you on this very day: I am clean of everyone’s blood,
for I did not shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God.
Pay careful attention to yourselves and to all the flock, in which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers,{j} to care for the church of God,{k} which he obtained with the blood of his own.{l}
I know that once I have gone, savage wolves will make their way in among you and will not spare the flock;
yes, out of your own number men will rise up uttering perversions, so as to lure the disciples away after themselves.
Keep awake, then, and remember that for a three-year stretch, by night and by day, I never stopped warning each of you, with tears.
And now I commend you to the Lord{m} and to the word of his grace, which is able to build you up and to give you the inheritance among all those who are sanctified.
I coveted no one’s silver or gold or apparel.
You yourselves know that these hands ministered to my necessities and to those who were with me.

In everything I have given you an example: that toiling thus we ought to come to the aid of the weak, keeping in mind the saying of the Lord Jesus himself, ‘More blessed is giving than receiving.’”{n}
And when he had said these things, he knelt down and prayed with them all.
They all wept freely, and falling on Paul’s neck they kissed him again and again,
grieved above all at the word he had said, that they were never more to see his face. Then they went with him down to the ship.

notes.text: Codex Bezae reads, “he wished to sail to Syria, but the Spirit told him to return through Macedonia.”
Gaius of Derbe: Codex Bezae reads “Gaius of Doberus,” a town in Macedonia, which would make him the Macedonian Gaius of 19:29.
Tychicus and Trophimus: Greek names, “fortunate” and “nourishing, foster child.” Many manuscripts add after “accompanied by” the words “as far as Asia.”
Eutychus: Greek, “fortunate.”
Third story: Greek *tristegou*.
Many later manuscripts add “at Trogyllium, and stayed there,” after “Samos.”
Our Lord Jesus: many manuscripts read “our Lord Jesus Christ.”
Constrained by the Spirit: or “bound in spirit.”

The text of this verse varies considerably among the manuscripts; many later ones read, “But none of these things move me, nor do I count my life dear to myself, so that I may finish my course with joy.”
Overseers: Greek *episkopous*, the word from which “bishop” derives.

The church of God: so the Westcott–Hort text, with Sinaiticus and Vaticanus. Many manuscripts, including Alexandrinus, Ephraemi, Codex Bezae, and the papyrus P74 (as reported), read “the church of the Lord,” and many later manuscripts conflate the two: “the church of the Lord and God.” The harder reading “of God” is generally preferred.

With the blood of his own: or “with his own blood.” Westcott and Hort suggested the meaning is “with the blood of his own [Son],” taking *tou idiou* as a title; many later manuscripts read “with his own blood” in a different word order.
The Lord: many manuscripts read “God.”
This saying of Jesus is not recorded in the Gospels.
